Neonates with sepsis are often brought in for evaluation due to poor feeding, inconsolability, or lethargy. Temperature instability causing either fever or hypothermia (<36 C [96.8 F]), is common although patients may be normothermic, as seen in this neonate. An abnormal leukocyte count (increased or decreased) or elevated immature neutrophil count (bands) is also concerning for sepsis.

Hemodynamically stable neonates with suspected sepsis warrant a full evaluation with a complete blood count, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis, urinalysis, and cultures of all 3 fluids (blood, urine, CSF). Patients should then receive empiric antibiotics with ampicillin, which targets GBS and L monocytogenes, along with gentamicin, which covers E coli and also acts synergistically with ampicillin against GBS and L monocytogenes. Acyclovir is often included in the empiric treatment regimen to cover herpes simplex virus.
educationalObjective: Neonatal sepsis typically causes nonspecific symptoms, including irritability, poor feeding, and lethargy. An abnormal leukocyte count is common. Empiric therapy is intravenous ampicillin and gentamicin to treat the most common pathogens, including group B Streptococcus, Escherichia coli, and Listeria monocytogenes.

stem: A 45-year-old man comes to the office due to a month of intermittent bloody diarrhea and abdominal pain and a 4-kg (9-lb) unintentional weight loss. The patient has no dizziness or chest pain. He was diagnosed with HIV a year ago after several years of intravenous heroin use. The patient does not take antiretroviral treatment consistently and no longer uses recreational drugs. He is currently engaged to an HIV-negative woman. The patient has never traveled abroad. Temperature is 38 C (100.4 F), blood pressure is 114/68 mm Hg, and pulse is 96/min. The mucous membranes are moist, and moderate cervical lymphadenopathy is present. Abdominal examination shows mild tenderness in the left lower quadrant. Laboratory results are normal except for a CD4 count of 28/mm³ and a potassium count of 3.2 mEq/L. What is the most likely cause of this patient's diarrhea?

explanations.A: Cryptosporidiosis is a common cause of chronic, profuse, watery diarrhea in patients with AIDS who have CD4 counts <180/mm³. This pathogen does not typically cause bloody stools.
explanations.B: Correct. Frequent, small-volume bloody diarrhea, abdominal pain, low-grade fever, and weight loss in a patient with AIDS and CD4 <50/mm³ raise strong suspicion for cytomegalovirus (CMV) colitis.
explanations.C: Entamoeba histolytica can cause bloody stools and fever but most often is acquired during international travel in countries with poor sanitation. It is not a common opportunistic pathogen in patients with AIDS in the United States.
explanations.D: Giardia causes malabsorptive, watery diarrhea. It can become chronic and result in significant weight loss (10%-20% or more) in patients with AIDS. However, it does not typically cause bloody stools.
explanations.E: Herpes simplex is usually associated with painful esophagitis or genital lesions in patients with HIV. It is an uncommon cause of colitis compared with CMV.
explanations.F: Kaposi sarcoma (KS) of the gastrointestinal tract can cause hematochezia, but fevers would be less likely. AIDS-related KS is much more common among men who have sex with men than among other populations with HIV (eg, intravenous drug users).
explanations.G: Disseminated Mycobacterium avium complex infection can cause chronic diarrhea and weight loss; however, the diarrhea is typically watery, not bloody.

generalExplanation:
Patients with advanced AIDS are at high risk for infectious diarrhea due to a variety of opportunistic bacterial, viral, and protozoal pathogens. Although delineation of the underlying organism typically requires stool and blood evaluation, a specific diagnosis is often suspected based on the quality (eg, watery or bloody, small or large volume) and frequency of the diarrhea.

In this case, the presence of low-grade fever, abdominal pain, intermittent bloody stools, and a CD4 count <50/mm³ raises strong suspicion for cytomegalovirus (CMV) colitis. CMV is a common opportunistic pathogen in patients with untreated AIDS; it is most prone to attack the retina and gastrointestinal system. CMV colitis generally presents with progressive fatigue, low-grade fever, weight loss, and frequent, low-volume, bloody stools. As with other causes of diarrhea, hypokalemia may be present but is nonspecific.

Diagnosis is typically made using colonoscopy with biopsy (eosinophilic intranuclear and basophilic intracytoplasmic inclusions). Although most patients with CMV colitis have evidence of CMV viremia, the presence of viremia cannot be used to diagnose end-organ disease (because viremia can occur without end-organ damage). Treatment with ganciclovir improves symptoms, but patients require antiretroviral therapy to prevent relapse. All patients with active CMV also require an ocular examination to rule out concurrent retinitis.
educationalObjective: Patients with AIDS who have CD4 counts <50/mm³ are at high risk for infectious colitis with opportunistic bacterial, viral, and protozoal pathogens. Cytomegalovirus colitis should be suspected in those with frequent, small-volume, bloody stools and abdominal pain. Diagnosis is confirmed by colonoscopy with biopsy. Any patient with HIV who has active CMV disease requires ocular examination to rule out concurrent retinitis.

stem: A 12-day-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his parents due to poor feeding. The patient is exclusively breastfed but has been less interested in feeding since last night. He was born via scheduled repeat cesarean delivery. Maternal group B streptococcal screening was positive, but intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis was deferred due to the planned cesarean delivery. The pregnancy was otherwise unremarkable, and the infant had an uncomplicated nursery stay. The patient's 3-year-old brother attends day care and has had rhinorrhea and cough this week. Temperature is 35.1 C (95.2 F). Physical examination shows a hypotonic, lethargic infant with a full anterior fontanelle. Initial laboratory studies reveal a leukocyte count of 2,000/mm³ with 20% bands. During the evaluation, he becomes apneic and requires intubation. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's condition?

explanations.A: Correct. Group B Streptococcus is the most common cause of neonatal sepsis and meningitis; late-onset disease (age >1 week) is horizontally transmitted from colonized contacts and is not prevented by intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis.
explanations.B: Haemophilus influenzae type b can cause bacteremia and meningitis, as well as pneumonia and epiglottitis, in unvaccinated children. However, H influenzae is a rare cause of sepsis in newborns due to low prevalence and protective maternal antibodies.
explanations.C: Neonatal sepsis and meningitis due to Listeria monocytogenes are clinically indistinguishable from GBS. However, L monocytogenes is far less common. Furthermore, because L monocytogenes is transmitted transplacentally, infection is typically early onset (age <1 week) and there is usually a maternal history of flulike symptoms or gastroenteritis, neither of which is seen in this patient.
explanations.D: Neisseria meningitidis and Streptococcus pneumoniae are common causes of meningitis in children age >1 month but rare causes of sepsis or meningitis during the neonatal period.
explanations.E: Neisseria meningitidis and Streptococcus pneumoniae are common causes of meningitis in children age >1 month but rare causes of sepsis or meningitis during the neonatal period.
explanations.F: Symptomatic congenital toxoplasmosis presents at birth with chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus, jaundice, and hepatosplenomegaly, none of which are seen in this patient.

generalExplanation:
This patient's hypothermia, lethargy, and leukopenia with elevated bands are concerning for neonatal sepsis, a systemic bacterial infection in infants age <=28 days. His full fontanelle and apnea are also worrisome for meningitis. Group B Streptococcus (GBS) is the most common cause of neonatal sepsis and meningitis.

Early-onset GBS disease (age <1 week) is transmitted vertically by exposure of the infant to the maternal genital tract or infected amniotic fluid (due to bacterial ascension) during labor and delivery. The incidence of early-onset disease has decreased due to universal screening of pregnant women and administration of intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis (IAP) to GBS-colonized mothers. IAP is not necessary for planned cesarean delivery without labor or rupture of membranes because GBS transmission is low in such settings.

However, late-onset GBS disease (age >1 week), as is likely seen in this patient, is horizontally transmitted (eg, person to person on unwashed hands) via exposure to colonized contacts. Therefore, IAP has not changed the incidence of late-onset GBS disease. This infant was likely exposed to GBS at home from his colonized mother or another household contact.
educationalObjective: Group B Streptococcus is the most common cause of neonatal sepsis and meningitis. Prevention of early-onset infection includes maternal screening before delivery and intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis, but these measures do not decrease the risk of late-onset (age >1 week) infection.

stem: A 24-year-old man comes to the emergency department due to a few hours of fever with rigors, headache, and myalgias. While at an urgent care center last night, he was diagnosed with syphilis and received a dose of intramuscular benzathine penicillin G. The patient has a history of HIV infection, and a recent CD4 count was 540/mm³. He is not currently taking antiretroviral therapy and takes no other medications. He continues to have unprotected intercourse with several partners despite counseling. The patient does not use tobacco, alcohol, or illicit drugs. Temperature is 38 C (100.4 F), blood pressure is 90/60 mm Hg, and pulse is 110/min. The patient is diaphoretic and appears uncomfortable. A diffuse, faint, macular rash involving the palms and soles is present. Genital examination shows a nontender ulcer with induration and several enlarged inguinal lymph nodes. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's current condition?

explanations.A: Anaphylactic reactions typically occur within minutes (not several hours) after drug exposure. Although hypotension is frequently present, urticarial (not macular) rash and respiratory symptoms are usually prominent.
explanations.B: Coinfection with multiple sexually transmitted infections is common. However, gonococcus typically causes urethritis rather than posttreatment, acute-onset hypotension and systemic symptoms; it is not commonly associated with a macular rash.
explanations.C: Syphilis is universally susceptible to penicillin; therefore, treatment failures are primarily seen when alternate regimens (eg, doxycycline) are used instead of penicillin.
explanations.D: Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome occurs in patients with HIV within days or weeks of antiretroviral initiation. It is marked by a paradoxical worsening of concurrent infectious symptoms due to immune system improvement. This patient was not started on antiretroviral treatment.
explanations.E: Correct. The Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction is an acute febrile illness occurring within hours after initiating syphilis treatment, caused by rapid lysis of spirochetes releasing lipoproteins into the circulation.

generalExplanation:
This patient with primary syphilis (chancre) received a dose of penicillin G last night and now has the Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction. Approximately 10%-35% of patients with early syphilis develop this reaction following antibiotic therapy initiation. It is caused by the rapid destruction of spirochetes, which results in a release of large quantities of lipoproteins into the systemic circulation. Patients typically develop an acute febrile illness <12 hours after antibiotic initiation; symptoms can include fever, myalgias, rigors, sweating, hypotension, and worsened syphilitic rash (diffuse, macular, including palms and soles). Manifestations are usually self-limited and resolve spontaneously within 48 hours.

The Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction may also occur after the treatment of other spirochetes (eg, Borrelia burgdorferi) or atypical organisms (eg, Bartonella).
educationalObjective: The Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction is an acute, febrile reaction that commonly occurs <12 hours after initial treatment of syphilis. Symptoms include fever, headache, myalgias, rigors, sweating, hypotension, and worsening syphilitic rash (if present). Manifestations are self-limited and typically resolve spontaneously within 48 hours.

stem: A 16-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his mother due to a possible hand injury. She noticed that the patient's right hand was swollen and that he was not using it despite being right-handed. He has a history of oppositional defiant disorder and refuses to say how his hand was injured. Temperature is 38 C (100.4 F), blood pressure is 110/72 mm Hg, and pulse is 80/min. The dorsum of the right hand is swollen. There is erythema centered over the long finger metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joint, where there is a small, linear scab; the area is fluctuant on palpation, and passive movement of the joint elicits severe pain. Right hand x-ray reveals soft tissue swelling, no retained foreign body, and no underlying fractures or dislocations. Which of the following is the best next step in management of this patient?

options.B: Oral antibiotic therapy and outpatient follow-up
options.C: Oral nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and outpatient follow-up
options.D: Surgical irrigation and debridement of the MCP joint

explanations.A: Intraarticular glucocorticoid injections are commonly used to reduce inflammation due to arthritis. This patient's fever, recent MCP joint trauma, and clinical findings of erythema, swelling, and pain on passive joint movement are more consistent with septic arthritis (ie, joint infection), for which suppression of the immune inflammatory response (ie, steroids) is contraindicated.
explanations.B: Although this patient should receive antibiotic therapy (eg, empiric IV antibiotics followed by culture-directed oral antibiotics) and pain control (eg, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs), urgent surgical intervention (vs outpatient follow-up) is required to drain the infected MCP joint and reduce the risk of permanent joint damage.
explanations.C: Although this patient should receive antibiotic therapy and pain control, urgent surgical intervention (vs outpatient follow-up) is required to drain the infected MCP joint and reduce the risk of permanent joint damage.
explanations.D: Correct. Septic arthritis of the MCP joint (often from a clenched-fist "fight bite" injury) requires urgent open surgical irrigation and debridement along with intravenous antibiotics.

generalExplanation:
This patient recently injured the tissue overlying his long finger metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joint and now has soft tissue swelling and erythema, fluctuance (likely representing trapped pus), severe pain with passive joint movement, and fever. This presentation is consistent with septic arthritis of the MCP joint and requires urgent surgical irrigation and debridement.

Infections of the long and ring finger MCP joints of the dominant hand (eg, right hand) are often caused by a clenched-fist punch to a human mouth ("fight bite"), which patients may be hesitant to disclose. Puncture (eg, tooth) through the thin soft tissue overlying the MCP joint inoculates the joint or its surrounding tissues with bacteria. The initial puncture wound may appear minor, but enclosed bacterial proliferation underneath the extensor tendon and/or within the joint capsule can quickly lead to septic arthritis, evidenced by swelling, erythema, fluctuance (or purulent drainage), and severe pain with passive range of motion.

All septic joints require drainage. Unlike larger joints (eg, knee), which can sometimes be drained via arthrocentesis or arthroscopy, the small MCP joints typically require open surgical irrigation and debridement. Intravenous (IV) antibiotics (eg, ampicillin/sulbactam) are started intraoperatively after obtaining joint cultures, and the wound is left open to drain and heal by secondary intention.
educationalObjective: Puncture of the thin soft tissue overlying the hand metacarpophalangeal joints (eg, clenched-fist punch to the human mouth) can result in septic arthritis, presenting with joint pain, erythema, swelling, fluctuance, and painful range of motion. Treatment requires urgent surgical irrigation and debridement and antibiotic therapy.

stem: A 2-year-old boy is brought to the clinic by his parents due to 6 days of high-grade fever and rash and a day of difficulty breathing. The rash began on the patient's face and subsequently spread to his trunk and extremities. Prior to the onset of rash, he had a nonproductive cough, tearing of eyes, runny nose, and intermittent nasal congestion. The family lives in a rural town in Zambia and is in the United States to visit relatives. The child has received no immunizations. Temperature is 38.7 C (101.7 F) and respirations are 44/min. Physical examination shows a diffuse erythematous, maculopapular rash all over the body that spares the palms and soles. Auscultation of the chest reveals bilateral crackles. The child is admitted to the local hospital for further care. Which of the following has been shown to reduce morbidity and mortality of patients with this infection?

explanations.A: Correct. Treatment with vitamin A reduces morbidity and mortality rates in children with severe measles (eg, those requiring hospitalization) by promoting antibody-producing cells and epithelial regeneration.
explanations.B: Vitamin B₆ (pyridoxine) deficiency can result in neurologic impairment (eg, confusion, irritability, seizure) and skin and mucous membrane breakdown (eg, stomatitis, cheilosis).
explanations.C: Vitamin B₁₂ (cobalamin) deficiency results in macrocytic anemia and hypersegmented neutrophils.
explanations.D: Vitamin E deficiency leads to hemolytic anemia and neurologic abnormalities such as ataxia.
explanations.E: Vitamin K deficiency causes coagulopathy and leads to easy bruising or bleeding from the mucosa and in deep tissues.

generalExplanation:
This unvaccinated child has a high fever and a diffuse morbilliform rash following a prodrome of cough, conjunctivitis, and coryza. These clinical findings are consistent with measles (rubeola). The rash characteristically begins on the face and spreads cephalocaudally. It lasts approximately a week, and patients' other symptoms improve as the rash resolves.

Treatment of measles is typically supportive only. However, patients who are immunocompromised or pregnant, at extremes of age (eg, infants or the elderly), or who are vitamin A deficient are at greater risk for complications such as pneumonia, encephalitis, or blindness. Treatment with vitamin A reduces the morbidity and mortality rates for patients with severe measles (eg, those requiring hospitalization) through the promotion of antibody-producing cells and regeneration of epithelial cells (eg, in the gut, lungs, and retina).
educationalObjective: The treatment of measles is supportive; however, vitamin A reduces morbidity and mortality rates in children with severe measles and should be administered to hospitalized patients.

stem:
A 25-year-old man comes to the office due to a positive home HIV test. The patient's partner was recently hospitalized with Pneumocystis pneumonia, which prompted the patient to get tested. He has no chronic medical conditions and takes no medications. He smokes a pack of cigarettes daily and uses intravenous heroin. The patient received all recommended childhood vaccinations through age 18. Vital signs are normal. Physical examination reveals no abnormalities. Laboratory results are as follows:

Hepatitis panel
  Hepatitis A virus antibody: negative
  Hepatitis B surface antibody (HBsAb): positive
  Hepatitis B core antibody (HBcAb): negative
  Hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg): negative
Antivaricella IgG antibody: negative
CD4 count: 440/mm³
HIV-1 RNA quantification (viral load): 22,000 copies/mL

Which of the following immunizations are recommended for this patient?

options.A: Hepatitis A: Yes; Pneumococcal: Yes; Zoster: Yes; Influenza: Yes
options.B: Hepatitis A: Yes; Pneumococcal: Yes; Zoster: No; Influenza: Yes
options.C: Hepatitis A: Yes; Pneumococcal: No; Zoster: Yes; Influenza: Yes
options.D: Hepatitis A: Yes; Pneumococcal: No; Zoster: No; Influenza: Yes
options.E: Hepatitis A: No; Pneumococcal: Yes; Zoster: Yes; Influenza: Yes
options.F: Hepatitis A: Yes; Pneumococcal: No; Zoster: Yes; Influenza: No

explanations.A: Correct. Patients with HIV who lack immunity should receive hepatitis A, pneumococcal (PCV13 followed by PPSV23), zoster (recombinant/inactivated), and annual inactivated influenza vaccines.
explanations.B: Zoster vaccination should be administered to those born after 1979 who have no evidence of immunity (as in this patient with negative anti-varicella IgG).
explanations.C: Patients with HIV should receive the 13-valent pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV13) followed by PPSV23 8 weeks later.
explanations.D: Both pneumococcal and zoster vaccinations are indicated in this patient with HIV.
explanations.E: Hepatitis A vaccination should be administered to those with no serologic evidence of immunity (and who are at increased risk, such as MSM or IV drug users).
explanations.F: Both pneumococcal and annual inactivated influenza vaccinations are indicated in this patient with HIV.

generalExplanation:
As with all adults, patients with HIV should receive vaccination for influenza annually in the fall (but with the inactivated formulation rather than the live attenuated or nasal formulations). They should also receive vaccination against the following pathogens due to elevated risk of infection or sequalae:
- Hepatitis A - vaccination should be administered to those with no serologic evidence of immunity.
- Hepatitis B - vaccination should be administered unless there is evidence of immunity (as in this patient with positive hepatitis B surface antibody and negative core/surface antigen) or active infection.
- Streptococcus pneumoniae - the 13-valent pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV13) should be administered, followed by the 23-valent pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine (PPSV23) 8 weeks later and again in 5 years and at age 65.
- Zoster - vaccination should generally be administered to those born after 1979 who have no evidence of immunity (as in this patient with negative anti-varicella IgG). The recombinant (inactivated) vaccine can be given to patients with CD4 counts <200/mm³ but the immunogenic response is often muted; therefore, it is frequently delayed until CD4 counts are improved following antiretroviral therapy initiation.
- Meningococcus - vaccination should be given to all patients with HIV and booster should be administered every 5 years.

Patients with HIV are also generally given revaccination for tetanus and diphtheria (Td) every 10 years; a single dose of tetanus-diphtheria-acellular pertussis (Tdap) is sometimes considered to address waning pertussis immunity, particularly in those who have not previously received Tdap.
educationalObjective: All adults should receive annual vaccination for influenza, as well as a single dose of tetanus-diphtheria-acellular pertussis, with revaccination for tetanus and diphtheria every 10 years. In addition, all patients with HIV should receive vaccinations for hepatitis A, hepatitis B, and zoster (unless they have documented immunity); immunization for Meningococcus and Streptococcus pneumoniae should also be given.

stem: A 63-year-old man comes to the office due to 2 days of increasing scrotal pain. The pain is worse with touch or movement and is not relieved by over-the-counter ibuprofen. The patient also has mild burning on urination and increased urinary frequency. He has a history of hypertension, erectile dysfunction, and type 2 diabetes mellitus. He takes tadalafil but no other medications. The patient is married and sexually active with his wife. He does not use tobacco or alcohol. Temperature is 38.1 C (100.8 F), blood pressure is 130/75 mm Hg, and pulse is 86/min. Physical examination shows a tender mass in the left scrotum that is mildly erythematous. Cremasteric reflex is intact. No urethral discharge is present. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's current condition?

explanations.A: Patients age <35 usually develop epididymitis due to sexually transmitted infections with Chlamydia trachomatis or Neisseria gonorrhoeae. These organisms often cause asymptomatic urethritis, so urinary symptoms occur less frequently.
explanations.B: Correct. In men age >35, acute epididymitis is most commonly caused by ascending coliform bacteria (such as Escherichia coli) related to bladder outlet obstruction.
explanations.C: Mumps virus usually causes a nonspecific prodrome (fever, malaise, myalgias) followed by parotitis. The most common complication is epididymo-orchitis, which is typically characterized by high fever and severe testicular pain. This patient did not have prodromal or parotid symptoms, making this diagnosis far less likely.
explanations.D: Patients age <35 usually develop epididymitis due to sexually transmitted infections with Chlamydia trachomatis or Neisseria gonorrhoeae.
explanations.E: Staphylococcus aureus can cause epididymitis or orchitis in the setting of a surgical procedure or severe overlying skin infection but is otherwise unlikely.

generalExplanation:
Acute epididymitis usually manifests with unilateral testicular pain and palpable swelling of the epididymis. The likely causative organism can often be predicted based on the age of the patient. Those age >35 most commonly develop epididymitis from bacteriuria related to bladder outlet obstruction (eg, benign prostate hyperplasia). Ascending coliform bacteria such as Escherichia coli are the most likely pathogens, and urinary tract inflammatory symptoms (eg, dysuria, frequency) are common.

Patients age <35 usually develop epididymitis due to sexually transmitted infections with Chlamydia trachomatis or Neisseria gonorrhoeae. These organisms often cause asymptomatic urethritis, so urinary symptoms occur less frequently.

Although patients of any age may engage in high-risk sexual behavior, this married 63-year-old man is far more likely to have a coliform bacterial infection than a sexually transmitted one.
educationalObjective: Acute epididymitis typically manifests with unilateral testicular pain and epididymal swelling. Those age >35 usually develop epididymitis due to bacteriuria from bladder outlet obstruction; ascending coliform organisms such as Escherichia coli are the most likely pathogens. Patients age <35 are far more likely to have epididymitis due to sexually transmitted infections with Chlamydia trachomatis or Neisseria gonorrhoeae.

stem: A 38-year-old man comes to the office due to 2 weeks of mildly pruritic and uncomfortable skin lesions. He first noticed a papule on his right index finger that soon ulcerated and began draining an odorless discharge. He then developed similar nodules on his right forearm. The patient has no prior medical problems. He drinks 1 or 2 cans of beer daily. He works as a landscaper and recently began living with his girlfriend, who owns a cat. Temperature is 36.9 C (98.4 F), blood pressure is 120/80 mm Hg, and pulse is 74/min. There is a nodular ulceration with nonpurulent drainage and surrounding erythema on the right index finger. Several proximal nontender subcutaneous nodules are palpable on his right forearm. No lymphadenopathy is present. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's current condition?

options.A: Bacterial inoculation from a reservoir cat
options.C: Filarial larvae transmitted by mosquito bite
options.E: Malignant skin transformation from sun exposure
options.F: Virus transmission from contact with body fluids

explanations.A: Cat scratch fever is marked by a cutaneous lesion (vesicular, erythematous, or papular) with prominent, tender, regional lymphadenopathy and possible systemic spread. This patient has no lymphadenopathy, making cat scratch fever unlikely.
explanations.B: Correct. Sporothrix schenckii is a dimorphic fungus found in decaying vegetation and soil that infects gardeners and landscapers, causing an ulcerating papule followed by proximal subcutaneous nodules along lymphatic channels.
explanations.C: Lymphatic filariasis is caused by a nematode that is endemic to Africa, Asia, Latin America, and some parts of the Caribbean. Patients with acute disease often have systemic symptoms (fever), painful lymphadenopathy, and lymphangitis. Chronic symptoms include disfiguring edema. This patient does not have fever, lymphangitis, or lymphadenopathy.
explanations.D: Hookworm larvae may cause a papular lesion at the site of entry (usually lower extremity) and proximal, intensely pruritic, reddish-brown tracks from larval migration. Multiple, nodular, ulcerating lesions that are mildly pruritic would be uncommon.
explanations.E: Skin cancer typically develops from lesions that have been present for years. This patient developed multiple lesions in 2 weeks, making malignancy unlikely.
explanations.F: Herpes simplex virus tends to cause painful vesicular lesions on an erythematous base, not nodular, ulcerating lesions with discharge.

generalExplanation: Sporothrix schenckii is a fungus found in decaying vegetation and soil. Infections occur via direct inoculation; landscapers and gardeners are primarily affected. A papule forms at the site of entry and soon ulcerates, draining an odorless, nonpurulent fluid. Several proximal lesions may develop along lines of lymphatic drainage. Infections rarely extend to deeper tissues or lymph nodes. Diagnosis requires aspiration or biopsy with culture. Treatment with several months of oral itraconazole is almost always curative.
educationalObjective: Sporothrix schenckii is a dimorphic fungus found in decaying plant matter and soil and primarily infects gardeners and landscapers (direct cutaneous inoculation). Typically, a papule forms at the inoculation site, which may ulcerate and drain nonpurulent, odorless fluid. Additional, proximal papular lesions may form along lines of lymphatic drainage. Deeper tissues and lymph nodes are usually spared, and systemic spread is rare.

stem: A 25-year-old man comes to the office due to a painless ulcer on his penis. He has no fever or urethral discharge. A few weeks ago, he had unprotected vaginal sex with a sex worker. The patient previously required hospitalization in the intensive care unit for toxic epidermal necrolysis after taking penicillin. He has no other medical conditions and takes no medications. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows a shallow, nontender, and nonexudative penile ulcer with a smooth base. Mild, bilateral inguinal lymphadenopathy is present. Serum rapid plasma reagin is positive, and HIV testing is negative. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for this patient?

explanations.A: Doxycycline is generally considered the best alternate treatment of primary syphilis due to ease of administration and efficacy. Although amoxicillin plus probenecid can also be used for primary syphilis, this patient with severe penicillin allergy should not be given amoxicillin.
explanations.B: Ciprofloxacin is effective against most gram-negative enteric organisms but has no efficacy against syphilis.
explanations.C: Clindamycin is often used to treat airway and skin aerobic and anaerobic infections, but it has no efficacy against syphilis.
explanations.D: Correct. Nonpregnant patients with primary syphilis and a severe penicillin allergy (eg, toxic epidermal necrolysis) should be treated with 14 days of oral doxycycline.
explanations.E: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole has fairly broad efficacy against gram-negative, gram-positive, and atypical organisms but does not effectively treat syphilis.

generalExplanation:
This patient had intercourse with a sex worker and subsequently developed a penile chancre (painless, nonexudative ulcer), inguinal lymphadenopathy, and a positive rapid plasma reagin (RPR) test, indicating primary syphilis. First-line treatment for primary syphilis is a single dose of intramuscular benzathine penicillin G, which provides therapeutic levels of penicillin for approximately 3 weeks. However, patients who are unable to take penicillin due to severe penicillin allergy can be treated with an alternate regimen such as 14 days of oral doxycycline or 10-14 days of intravenous or intramuscular ceftriaxone.

Alternate regimens are generally recommended for patients with severe penicillin allergy who have any stage of syphilis other than neurosyphilis; patients with neurosyphilis who have severe penicillin allergy usually require penicillin desensitization followed by administration of penicillin to ensure eradication of the organism (penicillin has 100% efficacy against the organism and excellent central nervous system penetration).

All patients with syphilis require nontreponemal titers (eg, RPR) at the time of treatment and again at 6-12 months to ensure adequate response (a 4-fold drop in titers). This is especially important for patients receiving alternate regimens because the risk of treatment failure is greater than in those who receive penicillin.
educationalObjective: Primary syphilis is treated with a single dose of intramuscular benzathine penicillin G; nonpregnant patients with severe penicillin allergy can receive 14 days of oral doxycycline.

stem:
A 48-year-old woman comes to the emergency department due to urinary frequency, burning pain on urination, severe nausea, and weakness. The patient has a history of type 2 diabetes mellitus treated with metformin. Her last menstrual period was a year ago, and she is not sexually active. Temperature is 38.3 C (101 F), blood pressure is 120/76 mm Hg, pulse is 95/min, and respirations are 14/min. The patient is obese. Mild costovertebral angle tenderness is present. Laboratory results are as follows:

Complete blood count
  Leukocytes: 12,000/mm³

Serum chemistry
  Blood urea nitrogen: 21 mg/dL
  Creatinine: 0.9 mg/dL
  Glucose: 118 mg/dL

Urinalysis shows many white blood cells. Intravenous ceftriaxone is started. Two days later, the patient feels better, is eating well, and is afebrile. Urine culture results show Escherichia coli sensitive to ceftriaxone, gentamicin, ciprofloxacin, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management of this patient?

explanations.A: This patient requires cessation of intravenous ceftriaxone as her symptoms are improved at 48 hours and urine culture shows sensitivity to oral antimicrobials. Adding ciprofloxacin without discontinuing ceftriaxone would not be recommended.
explanations.B: This patient requires cessation of intravenous ceftriaxone as her symptoms are improved at 48 hours and urine culture shows sensitivity to oral antimicrobials.
explanations.C: Pyelonephritis is a serious infection and usually requires 7-14 (not 3) days of antibiotics.
explanations.D: Intravenous gentamicin is occasionally used for pyelonephritis; however, this patient had a resolution of symptoms with ceftriaxone and therefore does not require an additional intravenous antimicrobial. She should be transitioned to an oral antibiotic.
explanations.E: Correct. After 48 hours of symptomatic improvement, hospitalized patients with pyelonephritis can be transitioned to culture-guided oral antimicrobials (eg, oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, a narrower-spectrum agent than ciprofloxacin) and discharged.

generalExplanation:
This patient with dysuria, pyuria, fever, and costovertebral angle tenderness has pyelonephritis. Management of pyelonephritis is guided by the clinical picture and comorbid conditions. Those with vomiting, older age, sepsis, and certain medical conditions (eg, diabetes mellitus, urinary obstruction) require hospitalization and intravenous antibiotics due to a higher risk of treatment failure with outpatient oral antibiotics.

After 48 hours of symptomatic improvement, most hospitalized patients can be transitioned to culture-guided oral antimicrobials. This patient with an Escherichia coli urinary infection sensitive to 2 oral agents can be switched to oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (a narrower-spectrum antibiotic than ciprofloxacin) and discharged.
educationalObjective: Patients with pyelonephritis who are vomiting, of older age, or septic or who have certain comorbidities (eg, diabetes mellitus, urinary obstruction) typically require hospitalization and intravenous therapy. Most hospitalized patients can be transitioned to culture-guided oral antibiotics if symptoms are improved at 48 hours.
